prize_parts.citation: For the development of general palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is the clearest case on the shortlist of a general method that changed how chemists everywhere build bonds. Buchwald and Hartwig independently turned a narrow, tin-dependent reaction into a general amination through ligand design (bulky biaryl and hindered alkyl phosphines), with the mechanistic work to explain why it works. The reaction is now a default disconnection in medicinal and process chemistry and is visible in thousands of syntheses and in large-scale manufacture. What was new chemically is easy to state: a predictable catalytic route to aryl amines under mild conditions. Attribution is clean at two names, and thirty years of use remove any maturity worry.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is originality relative to the 2010 cross-coupling prize: it can be read as the same Pd(0)/Pd(II) manifold extended to a new heteroatom, with the conceptual ground already recognised. Kosugi's earlier tin-amide coupling is a real precursor, and I am working from memory on how far it anticipated the catalytic cycle. The credited-name list also puts Kosugi outside a two-person prize, which would be a deliberate narrowing.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks C-N coupling first as a new bond-forming capability with decades of demonstrated consequences, treating Kosugi as a less general precursor.
responses.response: I agree and it is my own first choice. Kosugi's work is a priority footnote, not a competing claim to the general method, because the substrate scope, ligand control and mechanism that made the reaction routine came from Buchwald and Hartwig. I share the worry about the 2010 prize but think the new heteroatom coupling, with its different mechanistic problem (amido reductive elimination), is a distinct advance.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing first as a deaminase chemistry turned into a programmable tool, with Liu as intellectual driver and Komor and Gaudelli as lead experimentalists.
responses.response: I take the point that it is conceptually clean and impactful, but I ask what was new chemically. Cytidine and adenosine deamination are known enzyme reactions, and the invention is the fusion architecture plus, for the adenine editor, directed evolution of a deaminase to act on DNA. That is high-quality protein engineering, closer to biology than to molecule-making. I would not oppose it as a prize but I do not see it as chemistry's core, and the credit split among Liu, Komor, Gaudelli and the Kondo/Nishida Target-AID work is less settled than Chabes suggests.

responses.point: Linke places base editing first and PROTACs second, arguing both are original, easily explained and open new capabilities, with PROTACs shifting pharmacology from occupancy to event-driven.
responses.response: I accept that PROTACs are conceptually generative and chemically demanding in ternary-complex design, which is why I rank B012 sixth rather than lower. My reservation is attribution and maturity: the shortlist carries eight names across PROTAC and glue strands, and Handa/Ito on cereblon do not fit neatly with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli. Until there is a cleaner three-name story and a stronger approved-drug record I prefer the older, proven method. If the committee wants a biology-facing prize this year, B012 is a serious second choice for me.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks massively parallel sequencing first because its reversible-terminator and pyrosequencing chemistry changed biology and medicine with quantifiable impact.
responses.response: The impact is beyond dispute and the terminator chemistry is real chemistry. My difficulty is attribution: Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Rothberg, Ju and Mayer all have credible claims and a three-name cap forces arbitrary exclusions. I would also want the chemical contribution (nucleotide design) isolated from instrumentation and engineering. I am open to it but not persuaded yet.

responses.point: Zou ranks molecular-sieve catalyst design first, describing it as architecture determining function with broad industrial reach in refining and emissions control.
responses.response: This is core chemistry and its industrial footprint is large, so I take it seriously. I did not place it on my ranking because credit is spread over several laureate-grade people (Corma, Davis, Zones, Yu, Tsapatsis) and the arc is long and diffuse, so no single transformative step is easy to cite. If the committee can agree on a tight citation, for example organic structure-directing agents, I would listen, but it is not my leading case.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards C-N coupling as too close to the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
How decisive Kosugi's earlier tin-amide coupling was, which I am recalling from memory rather than from verified literature.
Whether a molecule-making prize is preferred this year over a chemical-biology or tools prize, given the strength of base editing and degraders in the opening ballots.
Whether the PROTAC credit can be cleanly drawn at three names.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from my profile for B055. I have no direct tie to Buchwald, Hartwig or Kosugi; I note only that I am the committee's sole synthetic organic chemist, which shapes my weighting.
